newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dealers see further fall in Russian yields.
newsitem.headline: Dealers see further fall in Russian yields.

text.p: Massive demand at Wednesday's auction of six-month GKO Treasury bills showed banks expected a further fall in the yields, dealers said.
The average yield on a 287-day T-bill fell to 45.01 percent from 53.08 percent at an auction of 259-day paper on November 13. Both issues are officially classified as six-month paper.

"There turned out to be more money in the system than we had expected," said Sergei Koshelenko, a dealer from CS First Boston. "People understood that long-term paper is of the most value and started increasing maturities."
The yield on a new 105-day tranche of six-month bills was 40.35 percent after 38.01 percent at an auction of a 56-day tranche last Wednesday.
Demand was so strong that the central bank was able to break with the policy it has followed since the late summer of simply raising enough to cover bill repayments.
Proceeds from the two auctions totalled 7.63 trillion roubles, well in excess of the 6.33 trillion roubles the finance ministry was repaying in maturing bills.

Ilya Savkin, an Alfa-Bank dealer, said that market participants felt cornered as the central bank planned to announce its hard currency policy next week, while investment in T-bills protected banks from inflation.

"Everyone is waiting to see what kind of rouble corridor will be announced and if we get less then 10 percent in hard currency when yields are 40 percent, everyone will invest in T-bills," said Anton Sukhoverko, a dealer from Mezhdunarodny Moskovsky Bank.
Savkin said demand from Western investors was medium and Russian banks made the most impact on the market.

"Previously T-bills were superattractive for investment," he said. "Now they are just attractive. You won't get a higher rate anywhere. I think we shall see a 35 percent yield on the longest-term paper in the near future."
Dealers said prices of long-term paper would continue rising on Thursday and said they expected a rise of about one percentage point.
"The growth will be a big one and we shall see a 42-43 percent yield on long-term paper," Sukhoverko said.
